manifest.subject: Biology
manifest.central_question: How do flowering plants (angiosperms) carry out sexual reproduction — from the formation of pollen grains and the embryo sac, through pollination and double fertilisation, to the development of the seed and fruit?
in_scope_units: 1.1 Flower — A Fascinating Organ of Angiosperms: introduces the flower as the site of sexual reproduction, with androecium (stamens) as the male reproductive whorl and gynoecium (pistils) as the female reproductive whorl.

1.2.1 Stamen, Microsporangium and Pollen Grain: structure of the stamen (filament, anther), the dithecous/tetragonal anther with four microsporangia, the four wall layers of the microsporangium (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum), microsporogenesis from sporogenous tissue/pollen mother cell to microspore tetrads, and the structure, wall layers (exine/intine) and viability of the mature pollen grain.

1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac: structure of the pistil (stigma, style, ovary), structure of a typical anatropous ovule (funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus), megasporogenesis from the megaspore mother cell, and monosporic development of the 8-nucleate, 7-celled female gametophyte (embryo sac) with egg apparatus, antipodals and polar nuclei.

1.2.3 Pollination: kinds of pollination (autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy), chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers, abiotic agents (wind, water) and biotic agents (animals) of pollination, outbreeding devices, and pollen-pistil interaction including emasculation and bagging techniques used in plant breeding.

1.3 Double Fertilisation: entry of the pollen tube into the synergid, discharge of the two male gametes, syngamy (fusion with the egg to form the diploid zygote) and triple fusion (fusion of the second male gamete with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus), together called double fertilisation.
1.4.1 Endosperm: free-nuclear endosperm development from the primary endosperm cell, cellularisation, and the fate of endosperm in albuminous versus non-albuminous seeds.

1.4.2 Embryo: stages of dicot embryogeny (proembryo, globular, heart-shaped, mature embryo), parts of a typical dicot embryo (embryonal axis, cotyledons, epicotyl, plumule, hypocotyl, radicle) and of a monocot embryo (scutellum, coleoptile, coleorrhiza).

1.4.3 Seed: structure of the seed (seed coat, cotyledons, embryonal axis), albuminous and non-albuminous seeds, perisperm, development of the fruit (pericarp) from the ovary, true fruits versus false fruits, and parthenocarpy.

1.5 Apomixis and Polyembryony: apomixis as a form of asexual reproduction that produces seeds without fertilisation, polyembryony (more than one embryo in a seed), and their importance in the hybrid seed industry.
banned_topics: Human male and female reproductive system anatomy, gametogenesis (spermatogenesis/oogenesis), menstrual cycle, fertilisation and implantation in humans, pregnancy and parturition — these belong to Chapter 2, Human Reproduction.
Reproductive health topics such as contraceptive methods, MTP, STIs and infertility/ART — these belong to Chapter 3, Reproductive Health.
Mendelian laws of inheritance, monohybrid/dihybrid crosses, chromosomal theory of inheritance and genetic disorders — these belong to Chapter 4, Principles of Inheritance and Variation.
DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation and the genetic code — these belong to Chapter 5, Molecular Basis of Inheritance.

known_pitfalls.claim: Meiosis takes place inside the pollen grain after it is released from the anther.
known_pitfalls.correction: Meiosis (microsporogenesis) occurs earlier, inside the microsporangium, when the diploid pollen mother cell (a sporogenous cell) divides meiotically to form a microspore tetrad. The pollen grain itself is already a haploid product of this division; inside the pollen grain, only mitotic division of the generative cell (to form two male gametes) may occur, never meiosis.

known_pitfalls.claim: Double fertilisation means two sperms fuse with the egg cell to form the zygote.
known_pitfalls.correction: Double fertilisation refers to two DIFFERENT fusion events happening in the same embryo sac: syngamy, where one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote, and triple fusion, where the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN). Only one male gamete fuses with the egg.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mature embryo sac is 8-celled because it has 8 nuclei.
known_pitfalls.correction: The mature angiosperm embryo sac is 8-nucleate but only 7-celled, because the two polar nuclei remain together, uncellularised, inside one large central cell rather than becoming two separate cells.

known_pitfalls.claim: The pollen grain wall is made entirely of cellulose, like a plant cell wall.
known_pitfalls.correction: The pollen grain has a two-layered wall: the hard outer exine is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known (it can withstand high temperature and strong acids/alkalis), while only the inner wall, the intine, is a thin layer of cellulose and pectin.

known_pitfalls.claim: A fruit can only form if fertilisation has taken place.
known_pitfalls.correction: While most fruits are the result of fertilisation, some species produce parthenocarpic fruits that develop from the ovary without fertilisation (e.g., banana); such fruits are seedless and parthenocarpy can also be induced artificially using growth hormones.

recommended_example_progression: Using the transverse section of a young anther (Figure 1.3a, b), trace the ploidy of cells from sporogenous tissue -> pollen mother cell -> microspore tetrad -> pollen grain.
Using the diagrammatic anatropous ovule (Figure 1.7d), identify and relate funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza and nucellus.

Using Figure 1.8 (b, c), trace the free-nuclear divisions of the functional megaspore through the 2-, 4- and 8-nucleate stages to the mature 7-celled embryo sac, based on the chapter's explanation of monosporic development.
Using Figure 1.13 (fertilised embryo sac showing zygote and PEN), work out the ploidy of the zygote (from syngamy) versus the primary endosperm nucleus (from triple fusion).
Using end-of-chapter Exercise 3, arrange 'pollen grain, sporogenous tissue, microspore tetrad, pollen mother cell, male gametes' into the correct developmental sequence.
manifest.ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter's EXERCISES section (numbered 1-18, pages 24-25) covers gametophyte development, pollination types, self-incompatibility, bagging/emasculation, double/triple fusion, embryo terminology, and false fruits/apomixis.

# Concept introduction: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

## What you will learn
You will learn why the flower is called the site of sexual reproduction in angiosperms, and you will be introduced to the two reproductive whorls of a flower — the androecium and the gynoecium — that will be studied in detail through the rest of this chapter.

## Simple explanation
Every flowering plant you see around you — from a hibiscus in a garden to a mango tree — reproduces sexually through its flowers. Flowers are not just decorative; they are morphological and embryological marvels that exist to bring about fertilisation and produce the fruits and seeds through which the species survives generation after generation. Reproduction is a vital process because, while individual organisms eventually die, species survive over millions of years only if they keep reproducing. Sexual reproduction, in particular, creates new variants and so improves survival advantage. A typical flower has four whorls, but the two that matter for sexual reproduction are the androecium (the male whorl, made up of stamens) and the gynoecium (the female whorl, made up of one or more pistils).

## Step-by-step breakdown
- **Flowers as the seat of sexual reproduction**: The chapter opens by pointing out that the diversity of flowers, their colours, scents and shapes are all adaptations that aid sexual reproduction, ensuring the formation of the end products of sexual reproduction, the fruits and seeds. Flowers also carry aesthetic, ornamental, social, religious and cultural value for humans.
- **Androecium — the male reproductive whorl**: The androecium consists of a whorl of stamens, which represent the male reproductive organs of the flower. Each stamen will later be shown to produce pollen grains, the male gametophytes.
- **Gynoecium — the female reproductive whorl**: The gynoecium represents the female reproductive organ of the flower and is made up of pistils. Depending on the species, the gynoecium may have a single pistil (monocarpellary) or more than one pistil (multicarpellary); when there is more than one pistil they may be fused together (syncarpous) or remain free (apocarpous).
- **Setting up the rest of the chapter**: Because both the male gametes (inside the pollen grain) and the female gamete (inside the embryo sac) are non-motile, the rest of the chapter systematically works through: how pollen grains and the embryo sac are formed (pre-fertilisation events), how pollen reaches the stigma (pollination), how the two types of gametes actually fuse (double fertilisation), and what happens to the ovule and ovary afterwards (post-fertilisation events, ending in seed and fruit).

## Worked example
Question: Based on Figure 1.1 (L.S. of a flower) referred to at the start of the chapter, name the two parts of a flower in which the two most important units of sexual reproduction develop, and state which whorl each belongs to.

Solution:
- The chapter asks the reader to recall the parts of a typical flower and identify where the male and female units of sexual reproduction develop.
- The stamen (part of the androecium) is where the male gametophyte, the pollen grain, develops inside the anther.
- The pistil (part of the gynoecium), specifically the ovule inside the ovary, is where the female gametophyte, the embryo sac, develops.
- Final answer: The two most important units of sexual reproduction develop in the anther of the stamen (androecium) and the ovule of the pistil (gynoecium).

## Common mistake
A common mistake is to think the 'flower' as a whole is the reproductive unit in the same way an animal has a single reproductive organ. In fact, the flower has two separate whorls doing separate jobs: the androecium (stamens) produces the male gametophyte (pollen grain), and the gynoecium (pistil) produces the female gametophyte (embryo sac) inside the ovule — both whorls must be studied and understood separately before their products can be brought together at fertilisation.

## Quick check question
Question: In a multicarpellary gynoecium, what is the difference between a syncarpous and an apocarpous condition?
Answer: In a syncarpous gynoecium the multiple pistils are fused together, whereas in an apocarpous gynoecium the multiple pistils remain free (separate) from one another.
Explanation: The chapter states that when a gynoecium has more than one pistil (multicarpellary), the pistils may be fused together (syncarpous, as in Papaver) or may be free (apocarpous, as in Michelia); this is a direct definitional distinction given with Figure 1.7 (b, c).

## Summary
- Flowers are the site of sexual reproduction in angiosperms.
- The androecium (whorl of stamens) is the male reproductive part of the flower.
- The gynoecium (made of one or more pistils) is the female reproductive part of the flower.
- A gynoecium can be monocarpellary (one pistil) or multicarpellary (many pistils, which may be syncarpous or apocarpous).
- This sets up the rest of the chapter: formation of male and female gametophytes, pollination, double fertilisation, and seed/fruit formation.
lessons.Core explanation:
# Core explanation: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

## What you will learn
You will learn the detailed structure of the stamen and how it produces pollen grains (microsporogenesis), the detailed structure of the mature pollen grain, and the detailed structure of the pistil/ovule and how it produces the embryo sac (megasporogenesis and monosporic development).

## Simple explanation
This is the heart of 'pre-fertilisation structures and events': before any fertilisation can happen, the plant must first build its male gametophyte (the pollen grain) inside the anther, and its female gametophyte (the embryo sac) inside the ovule. Both processes begin with a diploid mother cell undergoing meiosis, but the details differ — the anther produces thousands of pollen grains from many pollen mother cells, while the ovule usually produces just a single functional embryo sac from one megaspore mother cell.

## Step-by-step breakdown
- **Structure of the stamen and anther**: A typical stamen has a long, slender stalk called the filament, and a terminal, generally bilobed structure called the anther. A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed, and each lobe has two theca, so the anther is described as dithecous; in transverse section it is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure with four microsporangia located at the corners, two in each lobe.
- **Wall layers of the microsporangium**: A microsporangium is generally surrounded by four wall layers: the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, and the innermost tapetum. The outer three layers protect the sporangium and help the anther dehisce to release pollen; the tapetum nourishes the developing pollen grains and its cells have dense cytoplasm and are often more than one nucleus.
- **Microsporogenesis**: When the anther is young, a group of compactly arranged homogenous cells called sporogenous tissue occupies the centre of each microsporangium. As the anther develops, cells of the sporogenous tissue (each a potential pollen/microspore mother cell) undergo meiosis to form microspore tetrads (a cluster of four haploid microspores) — this process is called microsporogenesis. As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores separate and develop into pollen grains, which are released when the anther dehisces.
- **Structure of the mature pollen grain**: Pollen grains (the male gametophytes) are generally spherical, about 25-50 micrometres in diameter, with a two-layered wall: a hard outer exine made of sporopollenin (one of the most resistant organic materials known, unaffected by high temperature or strong acids/alkalis, and with no known degrading enzyme), interrupted by germ pores where sporopollenin is absent; and a thin inner intine made of cellulose and pectin. A mature pollen grain contains a large vegetative cell with abundant food reserve, and a smaller, spindle-shaped generative cell floating in its cytoplasm; in over 60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage, while in the rest the generative cell divides mitotically to give two male gametes before shedding (3-celled stage).
- **Structure of the pistil and the ovule**: Each pistil has three parts: the stigma (landing platform for pollen), the style (the elongated slender part beneath the stigma), and the ovary (basal bulged part, containing the ovarian cavity/locule with the placenta). Ovules (megasporangia) arise from the placenta; a typical anatropous ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk, the funicle, and the region where the ovule body fuses with the funicle is the hilum. Each ovule has one or two protective integuments that encircle the nucellus except at the tip, where there is a small opening, the micropyle; opposite the micropylar end is the chalaza, the basal part of the ovule. The nucellus (enclosed within the integuments) has abundant reserve food and houses the embryo sac.
- **Megasporogenesis and monosporic development**: The formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC) is called megasporogenesis. Ovules generally differentiate a single MMC in the micropylar region of the nucellus; this large cell, with dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus, undergoes meiosis to produce four megaspores. In most flowering plants only one megaspore is functional while the other three degenerate — this is called monosporic development of the embryo sac.
- **Formation of the 8-nucleate, 7-celled embryo sac**: The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to form 2 nuclei (2-nucleate stage), then two more free-nuclear mitotic divisions produce the 4-nucleate and 8-nucleate stages (these nuclear divisions are not immediately followed by cell wall formation). After the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down: three cells at the micropylar end form the egg apparatus (two synergids with a filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube, plus one egg cell), three cells at the chalazal end are the antipodals, and the remaining two nuclei (the polar nuclei) share one large central cell — making the mature embryo sac 8-nucleate but only 7-celled.

## Worked example
Question: Based on the chapter's discussion of the anther (Figure 1.3), a young microsporangium contains sporogenous tissue with diploid (2n) cells. If one such cell undergoes microsporogenesis, what is the ploidy of the resulting microspore tetrad cells, and what will each mature into?

Solution:
- The sporogenous tissue cell that will divide is a pollen mother cell (PMC), and it is diploid because it has not yet undergone meiosis.
- Microsporogenesis is defined in the chapter as the formation of microspores from a PMC through meiosis.
- Since meiosis halves the chromosome number, each of the four cells of the microspore tetrad produced is haploid (n).
- Final answer: The microspore tetrad cells are haploid (n); as the anther matures, each microspore dissociates from the tetrad and develops into a pollen grain (the male gametophyte).

## Common mistake
A common mistake is to assume the tapetum is just another 'protective' layer like the epidermis or endothecium. In fact, the chapter distinguishes it clearly: the outer three wall layers (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers) perform protection and help dehiscence, while the tapetum — the innermost layer — has a completely different, nutritive role: it nourishes the developing pollen grains, and its cells are characteristically dense in cytoplasm and often multi-nucleate.

## Quick check question
Question: Why is the mature embryo sac described as '8-nucleate but 7-celled'?
Answer: Because although the functional megaspore's nucleus undergoes free-nuclear mitotic divisions to eventually give 8 nuclei, only 6 of these nuclei get separate cell walls (2 synergids + 1 egg cell at the micropylar end, and 3 antipodals at the chalazal end); the remaining 2 nuclei, the polar nuclei, stay together uncellularised inside one large central cell.
Explanation: This directly follows the chapter's description: 'Six of the eight nuclei are surrounded by cell walls and organised into cells; the remaining two nuclei, called polar nuclei are situated below the egg apparatus in the large central cell,' which is why the embryo sac, though 8-nucleate, is described as 7-celled.

## Summary
- A stamen has a filament and a bilobed, dithecous, tetragonal anther with four microsporangia.
- Each microsporangium has four wall layers (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum); the tapetum nourishes developing pollen.
- Microsporogenesis: sporogenous tissue -> pollen mother cell -> (meiosis) -> microspore tetrad -> pollen grains.
- The mature pollen grain has an exine (sporopollenin, with germ pores) and intine (cellulose/pectin) wall, and a vegetative cell plus a generative cell (2-celled or 3-celled stage).
- A pistil has stigma, style and ovary; the ovule has funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza and nucellus.
- Megasporogenesis: MMC undergoes meiosis to give four megaspores; monosporic development means only one is functional and forms the 8-nucleate, 7-celled embryo sac (egg apparatus, antipodals, central cell with polar nuclei).

# Worked examples: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

## What you will learn
You will learn the different kinds of pollination and pollinating agents, the devices flowering plants use to discourage self-pollination, how the pistil recognises compatible versus incompatible pollen (pollen-pistil interaction), and the emasculation/bagging techniques plant breeders use to control pollination.

## Simple explanation
Once pollen grains and the embryo sac are ready, the male gametes (inside the pollen grain) still need to physically reach the female gametes (inside the embryo sac), since neither is motile on its own. This is achieved by pollination — the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma — using either abiotic agents (wind, water) or biotic agents (mostly animals such as bees). Because most flowers are hermaphrodite, plants have also evolved several outbreeding devices to avoid constant self-pollination, and the pistil itself has a chemical 'dialogue' with pollen grains to accept or reject them.

## Step-by-step breakdown
- **Kinds of pollination**: Autogamy is pollination within the same flower (transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower); it requires synchrony between pollen release and stigma receptivity, and the anther and stigma lying close together. Geitonogamy is transfer of pollen to the stigma of another flower of the same plant — functionally cross-pollination (it needs a pollinating agent) but genetically equivalent to autogamy since the pollen still comes from the same plant. Xenogamy is transfer of pollen to the stigma of a genetically different plant, and is the only type that brings genetically different pollen to the stigma.
- **Chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers**: Some plants such as Viola, Oxalis and Commelina produce chasmogamous flowers (with exposed anthers and stigma, like most flowers) as well as cleistogamous flowers, which never open at all. In cleistogamous flowers the anther and stigma lie so close that pollen contacts the stigma while still inside the bud, making autogamy certain and giving assured seed-set even without pollinators — but with no chance of cross-pollen ever landing on the stigma.
- **Abiotic agents of pollination**: Wind-pollinated flowers typically have light, non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, and large, often feathery stigmas to trap airborne pollen (e.g., the stigma and style of a corn cob); they often have a single ovule per ovary and many flowers packed into an inflorescence, and produce huge amounts of pollen because pollen landing on a stigma is a matter of chance. Water pollination is rare, limited to about 30 genera (mostly monocots) such as Vallisneria and Hydrilla (freshwater) and Zostera (marine); in most aquatic plants (e.g., water hyacinth, water lily) flowers instead emerge above water and are pollinated by insects or wind.
- **Biotic agents of pollination**: Most flowering plants use animals — bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, humming birds) and bats — as pollinating agents, with insects (especially bees) being dominant. Insect-pollinated flowers are usually large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar (or clustered into a conspicuous inflorescence if individually small); flowers pollinated by flies/beetles instead secrete foul odours. Animals are rewarded with nectar and/or pollen, and in some cases (e.g., Amorphophallus, or the Yucca-moth relationship) even with a safe place to lay eggs.
- **Outbreeding devices**: Because continued self-pollination causes inbreeding depression, flowering plants have evolved devices to discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination: lack of synchrony between pollen release and stigma receptivity; anther and stigma placed at different positions (both of these prevent autogamy); self-incompatibility, a genetic mechanism that inhibits pollen germination or pollen tube growth of self-pollen in the pistil; and production of unisexual flowers — monoecious plants (male and female flowers on the same plant, e.g., castor, maize) prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy, while dioecious plants (male and female flowers on different plants, e.g., papaya) prevent both autogamy and geitonogamy.
- **Pollen-pistil interaction**: The pistil can recognise whether pollen landing on the stigma is of the compatible (right) type or incompatible (wrong) type, through a chemical dialogue between pollen and pistil components; compatible pollen is accepted and promotes post-pollination events leading to fertilisation, while incompatible pollen is rejected by preventing germination on the stigma or pollen tube growth in the style. All events from pollen landing on the stigma until the pollen tube enters the ovule are together called pollen-pistil interaction.
- **Emasculation and bagging in artificial hybridisation**: To control which pollen fertilises which plant in a breeding programme: if the female parent has bisexual flowers, its anthers are removed before dehiscence using forceps — this step is emasculation; the emasculated flower is then covered with a bag (bagging) to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen. When the stigma becomes receptive, the desired pollen is dusted on it and the flower is rebagged. If the female parent has unisexual flowers, emasculation is unnecessary — only the female flower buds are bagged before opening, then pollinated with the desired pollen and rebagged.

## Worked example
Question: A plant breeder wants to cross a bisexual flower (female parent) with pollen from a chosen male parent, to guarantee a controlled hybrid cross. Describe, in the correct order, the two techniques the breeder must use and why each is necessary.

Solution:
- Because the female parent's flower is bisexual, it carries its own anthers, so left alone it could self-pollinate before the breeder can apply the desired pollen.
- The breeder must first perform emasculation: removing the anthers of the flower bud with forceps before they dehisce, so the flower cannot pollinate itself.
- The emasculated flower must then be covered using the bagging technique (typically with a butter-paper bag) to prevent any unwanted/contaminating pollen from landing on the now-receptive stigma.
- Once the stigma becomes receptive, the breeder dusts on mature pollen collected from the anthers of the chosen male parent, and rebags the flower to let the fruit develop.
- Final answer: The breeder must emasculate the female parent flower (remove its own anthers) and then bag it to prevent contamination, before manually applying the desired pollen and rebagging — this ensures the resulting seeds are a true controlled hybrid cross.

## Common mistake
A common mistake is to think geitonogamy is genetically the same as xenogamy simply because a pollinating agent (like a bee) is involved in both. The chapter is explicit that geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination (it needs a pollinating agent to carry pollen from one flower to another) but genetically it is equivalent to autogamy, since the pollen still comes from the same plant. Only xenogamy brings genetically different pollen to the stigma.

## Quick check question
Question: Why do wind-pollinated and water-pollinated flowers typically lack bright colours and nectar, while insect-pollinated flowers are usually large, colourful and fragrant?
Answer: Because wind and water are abiotic (non-living) agents that do not need to be attracted — they simply carry pollen mechanically wherever the air or water current takes it, so such flowers instead invest in features like light, non-sticky pollen and exposed stamens/feathery stigmas. Insects and other animals, however, are living pollinators that must be lured to visit the flower and be given a reward (nectar or pollen), which is why insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and nectar-rich.
Explanation: The chapter explains that pollen landing on the stigma is a chance factor in wind and water pollination, so such flowers instead compensate by producing enormous amounts of pollen, whereas animal-pollinated flowers must actively attract their pollinators by colour, fragrance and rewards (nectar/pollen) since the animal must be induced to visit and make contact with the anther and stigma.

## Summary
- Pollination types by source of pollen: autogamy (same flower), geitonogamy (different flower, same plant, genetically like autogamy), xenogamy (different plant, genetically distinct pollen).
- Cleistogamous flowers never open and are always autogamous; chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers/stigma.
- Abiotic pollination uses wind (common) or water (rare, ~30 genera); biotic pollination by animals (mainly insects/bees) is most common overall.
- Outbreeding devices — asynchrony, spatial separation of anther/stigma, self-incompatibility, and unisexuality (monoecy/dioecy) — reduce inbreeding.
- Pollen-pistil interaction lets the pistil accept compatible pollen and reject incompatible pollen.
- Emasculation (removing anthers) and bagging (isolating the stigma) are used together by breeders to control artificial hybridisation.

# Exam-style problems: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

## What you will learn
You will learn what happens immediately after the pollen tube enters the embryo sac — the two fusion events that make up double fertilisation — and everything that follows: development of the endosperm, development of the embryo, and maturation of the ovule into a seed and the ovary into a fruit.

## Simple explanation
After a compatible pollen tube grows down the style and enters a synergid, it releases its two male gametes. What happens next is unique to flowering plants: two separate fusion events occur in the same embryo sac, together called double fertilisation. This single event triggers a cascade of post-fertilisation changes — the primary endosperm cell starts dividing to nourish the embryo, the zygote develops through defined stages into a mature embryo, and the whole ovule matures into a seed while the ovary matures into a fruit.

## Step-by-step breakdown
- **Double fertilisation: syngamy and triple fusion**: After the pollen tube discharges its two male gametes into the cytoplasm of a synergid, one male gamete moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus — this fusion, called syngamy, forms the diploid zygote. The other male gamete moves to the two polar nuclei in the central cell and fuses with both of them to produce a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN); because this fusion involves three haploid nuclei, it is called triple fusion. Since two types of fusion (syngamy and triple fusion) occur in the same embryo sac, the whole phenomenon is termed double fertilisation, an event unique to flowering plants.
- **Fate of the central cell and zygote**: After triple fusion, the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC), which develops into the endosperm, while the zygote develops into the embryo. All events from here on — endosperm and embryo development, and maturation of ovule(s) into seed(s) and ovary into fruit — are together called post-fertilisation events.
- **Endosperm development**: Endosperm development precedes embryo development, since the endosperm provides nutrition for the growing embryo. The primary endosperm cell divides repeatedly to form triploid endosperm tissue filled with reserve food. In the most common pattern, the PEN first undergoes successive free-nuclear divisions (free-nuclear endosperm — e.g., the liquid coconut water in a tender coconut, made of thousands of free nuclei) before cell walls form, making it cellular (the white kernel of a coconut is cellular endosperm). Endosperm may be completely used up by the developing embryo before seed maturation (non-albuminous seeds, e.g., pea, groundnut, beans) or may persist in the mature seed (albuminous seeds, e.g., castor, coconut) to be used during germination.
- **Embryo development (embryogeny)**: The embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac, where the zygote is located; most zygotes divide only after some endosperm has formed, ensuring assured nutrition for the embryo. Early stages of embryogeny (proembryo, globular, heart-shaped, and mature embryo) are similar in both monocots and dicots. A typical dicot embryo has an embryonal axis and two cotyledons; the part of the axis above the cotyledons is the epicotyl (ending in the plumule/stem tip), and the part below is the hypocotyl (ending in the radicle/root tip, covered by a root cap). A monocot embryo has only one cotyledon — in grasses called the scutellum — with the radicle and root cap enclosed in a sheath called the coleorrhiza, and the epicotyl bearing the shoot apex and leaf primordia enclosed in the coleoptile.
- **Structure of the seed**: A seed typically consists of seed coat(s), cotyledon(s), and an embryonal axis. Non-albuminous seeds (e.g., pea, groundnut) have no residual endosperm, since it is fully consumed during embryo development; albuminous seeds (e.g., wheat, maize, barley, castor) retain part of the endosperm. In some seeds (e.g., black pepper, beet) a residual, persistent nucellus called the perisperm is also present. The integuments harden into the seed coat, and the micropyle persists as a small pore that lets oxygen and water enter during germination; a mature seed's water content drops to about 10-15% by mass, and the embryo may enter dormancy or germinate if conditions (moisture, oxygen, temperature) are favourable.
- **Fruit formation, true and false fruits, and parthenocarpy**: As ovules mature into seeds, the ovary wall develops into the fruit wall, or pericarp (fleshy as in guava, orange, mango, or dry as in groundnut, mustard). Fruits that develop only from the ovary are true fruits; in a few species (e.g., apple, strawberry, cashew) the thalamus also contributes to the fruit, and these are called false fruits. Although most fruits result from fertilisation, some species (e.g., banana) form parthenocarpic fruits — seedless fruits that develop without fertilisation; parthenocarpy can also be artificially induced through growth hormones.

## Worked example
Question: Based on Figure 1.13 in the chapter (fertilised embryo sac showing zygote and PEN), if the egg cell and the two polar nuclei are all haploid before fertilisation, work out the ploidy of the zygote and the ploidy of the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) after double fertilisation, and name the fusion event responsible for each.

Solution:
- The egg cell is haploid (n); when one male gamete (also haploid, n) fuses with it in syngamy, the resulting zygote has n + n = 2n chromosomes, i.e., it is diploid.
- The central cell contains two polar nuclei, each haploid (n); when the second male gamete (n) fuses with both polar nuclei in triple fusion, the resulting primary endosperm nucleus has n + n + n = 3n chromosomes, i.e., it is triploid.
- This matches the chapter's statement that triple fusion involves the fusion of three haploid nuclei.
- Final answer: The zygote is diploid (2n), formed by syngamy (egg + 1 male gamete); the primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) is triploid (3n), formed by triple fusion (2 polar nuclei + 1 male gamete).

## Common mistake
A common mistake is to assume the embryo starts developing immediately after the zygote forms. The chapter specifically notes that most zygotes divide only after a certain amount of endosperm has already formed — this is an adaptation to ensure the developing embryo has assured nutrition, which is also why endosperm development precedes embryo development.

## Quick check question
Question: Differentiate between a non-albuminous seed and an albuminous seed, giving one example of each from the chapter.
Answer: A non-albuminous seed has no residual endosperm in the mature seed because it is completely consumed by the developing embryo (e.g., pea, groundnut); an albuminous seed retains part of the endosperm in the mature seed because it is not completely used up during embryo development, and this remaining endosperm is used later during germination (e.g., castor, wheat, maize, barley).
Explanation: The chapter directly defines these two seed categories based on whether the endosperm formed after triple fusion is fully consumed before seed maturation (non-albuminous) or persists into the mature seed (albuminous).

## Summary
- Double fertilisation = syngamy (egg + male gamete -> diploid zygote) + triple fusion (2 polar nuclei + male gamete -> triploid PEN), both occurring in the same embryo sac.
- The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell after triple fusion and develops into the endosperm; endosperm formation precedes and nourishes embryo development.
- A dicot embryo has two cotyledons, epicotyl (plumule) and hypocotyl (radicle); a monocot embryo has one cotyledon (scutellum), coleoptile and coleorrhiza.
- Seeds may be non-albuminous (endosperm fully used, e.g., pea) or albuminous (endosperm persists, e.g., castor); some seeds also retain a perisperm.
- The ovary wall becomes the pericarp of the fruit; true fruits develop from the ovary alone, false fruits also involve the thalamus (e.g., apple), and parthenocarpic fruits (e.g., banana) form without fertilisation.
lessons.Revision and recap:
# Revision and recap: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

## What you will learn
You will learn about apomixis and polyembryony, two special reproductive phenomena covered at the end of the chapter, and you will revise the entire chapter's flow from flower structure through pollination, double fertilisation, and seed/fruit formation.

## Simple explanation
Not every seed in nature is the result of the full sexual process you have just studied. Some flowering plants have evolved apomixis, a way of producing seeds without fertilisation at all, and some produce more than one embryo per seed (polyembryony). Both phenomena matter a great deal in modern agriculture, especially for maintaining hybrid crop varieties. This final step also pulls together the whole chapter, from the flower down to the fruit, so you can see how each pre-fertilisation, fertilisation, and post-fertilisation stage connects to the next.

## Step-by-step breakdown
- **Apomixis**: A few flowering plants (e.g., some species of Asteraceae and grasses) have evolved apomixis, a mechanism to produce seeds without fertilisation; apomixis is described as a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. In some species, the diploid egg cell forms without reduction division (meiosis) and develops directly into the embryo without fertilisation. In other cases, as in many Citrus and Mango varieties, nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac, and develop into embryos.
- **Polyembryony**: When more than one embryo occurs in a single seed, this is called polyembryony; it is commonly seen in species such as Citrus and Mango, where nucellar cells give rise to extra embryos alongside (or instead of) the zygotic embryo — for example, squeezing seeds of orange reveals several embryos of different sizes.
- **Why apomixis matters for agriculture**: Hybrid varieties of many food and vegetable crops are extensively cultivated because hybrid vigour increases productivity, but hybrid seeds must be produced fresh every year (since sowing seeds collected from a hybrid causes the progeny to segregate and lose hybrid characters), making hybrid seed production costly. If hybrids could be converted into apomicts, there would be no segregation of characters in the progeny, and farmers could reuse hybrid seeds year after year without buying new seed — this is why active research is ongoing into the genetics of apomixis.
- **Full chapter recap — pre-fertilisation**: The flower's androecium (stamens) produces pollen grains via microsporogenesis in the anther's microsporangia (with tapetum nourishing them), while the gynoecium (pistil) produces the embryo sac via megasporogenesis in the ovule's nucellus, resulting in monosporic development of the 8-nucleate, 7-celled female gametophyte.
- **Full chapter recap — pollination**: Pollen is transferred from anther to stigma by autogamy, geitonogamy or xenogamy, using abiotic (wind, water) or biotic (mostly insect) agents; outbreeding devices and pollen-pistil interaction help ensure only compatible pollen germinates and grows a pollen tube down to the ovule.
- **Full chapter recap — fertilisation and beyond**: The pollen tube enters a synergid and releases two male gametes, bringing about double fertilisation (syngamy giving the diploid zygote, and triple fusion giving the triploid PEN). The PEC develops into endosperm (non-albuminous or albuminous), the zygote develops through proembryo/globular/heart-shaped stages into a mature dicot or monocot embryo, the ovule matures into the seed, and the ovary matures into the fruit (true or false; sometimes parthenocarpic).

## Worked example
Question: Using the chapter's discussion of apomixis in Citrus and Mango, explain why apomictic embryos formed from nucellar cells are sometimes described as clones of the parent plant, and connect this to why apomixis is valuable for the hybrid seed industry.

Solution:
- In apomixis of the nucellar type (as in many Citrus and Mango varieties), the embryo arises from nucellar cells of the parent sporophyte, not from fusion of male and female gametes.
- Because these nucellar cells are diploid tissue of the mother plant produced by ordinary mitotic division, the embryo they give rise to has exactly the same genotype as the parent plant, with no genetic recombination — which is why such embryos can be considered clones.
- This means that if a hybrid variety could be made apomictic, its seeds would produce offspring genetically identical to the hybrid itself, with no segregation of characters, unlike normal hybrid seeds where sown progeny segregate and lose the hybrid combination.
- Final answer: Apomictic (nucellar) embryos are essentially clones because they are produced from the mother plant's own diploid tissue without fertilisation; this is exactly why converting hybrid crop varieties into apomicts is a major research goal — it would let farmers reuse hybrid seed every year without buying fresh hybrid seed and without losing the hybrid's superior characters.

## Common mistake
A common mistake is to think apomixis and polyembryony are the same phenomenon. They are related but distinct: apomixis is about how a seed forms (asexually, without fertilisation), while polyembryony is about how many embryos are present in one seed (more than one). In species like Citrus and Mango, both occur together because nucellar cells that give rise to apomictic embryos develop alongside the normal zygotic embryo in the same ovule/seed.

## Quick check question
Question: A farmer wants to keep sowing seeds saved from a high-yield hybrid crop every year, but is currently told that this doesn't work well with ordinary hybrid seeds. Based on the chapter, what property would the hybrid need to have for this to work, and why?
Answer: The hybrid would need to be converted into an apomict, i.e., it would need to reproduce via apomixis instead of ordinary sexual reproduction, so that its seeds develop without fertilisation and there is no segregation of characters in the progeny.
Explanation: The chapter explains that with ordinary hybrid seeds, sowing seeds collected from the hybrid causes the plants in the progeny to segregate and not maintain hybrid characters, making fresh hybrid seed production necessary (and costly) every year; if the hybrid were instead made apomictic, the farmer could keep reusing the same hybrid seed every year without buying new seed, since apomictic reproduction does not cause this segregation.

## Summary
- Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction (seed formation without fertilisation) that mimics sexual reproduction; it occurs via a diploid egg forming without reduction division, or via nucellar cells developing into embryos (as in Citrus, Mango).
- Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a single seed, often linked to apomixis via extra nucellar embryos.
- Apomixis is important in the hybrid seed industry because apomictic hybrids would not segregate in the next generation, saving farmers the cost of buying fresh hybrid seed every year.
- The full chapter arc: flower (androecium + gynoecium) -> pre-fertilisation (microsporogenesis/pollen grain and megasporogenesis/embryo sac) -> pollination -> double fertilisation -> post-fertilisation (endosperm, embryo, seed, fruit) -> apomixis/polyembryony as special exceptions.
- Seeds give angiosperms major advantages: reproduction independent of water, better dispersal, stored food for seedlings, a protective seed coat, and new genetic combinations from sexual reproduction.
